record.title: FTC proposes a Section 5 theory for undisclosed AI output steering
record.summary: On July 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission issued a proposed policy statement and requested comments by July 31 on how Section 5 deception principles apply when AI companies steer outputs away from what consumers reasonably expect without adequate disclosure. The proposal argues that undisclosed ideological output steering may deceive consumers and that state requirements that compel conflicting output changes may be impliedly preempted. A separate Colorado law addresses automated decision systems used for consequential decisions; the inspected statutory clauses do not themselves establish the output-steering premise described by the FTC. The proposal is not binding law or an adjudicated federal-state conflict. An October review found the proposal still listed on FTC pages but did not inspect the docket comments or establish a final disposition.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: On July 1, 2026, the FTC announced a proposed policy statement on AI output accuracy and requested public comments by July 31; the Commission vote authorizing the Federal Register notice was 2-0.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The proposed FTC statement argues that steering AI outputs toward undisclosed ideological objectives may deceive consumers under Section 5 and that state requirements compelling conflicting output changes may be impliedly preempted. This is a proposed agency interpretation, not binding law or an adjudicated conflict.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Colorado SB26-189 contains duties concerning covered automated decision technology used in consequential decisions, including disclosures, correction rights and meaningful human review. The inspected statutory clauses do not themselves establish that the law requires AI outputs to be distorted toward ideological objectives; the source comparison does not settle preemption or every application.

evidence_gaps.description: Comments on docket FTC-2026-0859 and any Commission response or final disposition were not inspected; Regulations.gov was inaccessible and FederalRegister.gov blocked the direct page in this pass.

The proposal’s implied-preemption theory has not been adjudicated, and the bounded comparison with Colorado SB26-189 does not establish the full scope of statutory conflict or any court/agency application.
No evidence shows whether the proposal changes provider disclosures, model output behavior, compliance costs, consumer understanding or enforcement.

brief.importance_rationale: If adopted and applied as described, this policy could materially affect AI companies’ disclosure incentives and federal-state regulatory relationships across a broad product market. Consequence is substantial but below field-shaping because the reviewed record is a proposed nonbinding policy statement, not a final rule, adjudication or demonstrated enforcement outcome.
limitations: The FTC document is expressly proposed and requested public comment; it is not binding law, a final rule or an adjudication.
The output-steering theory and implied-preemption argument are agency claims; neither is established as the governing interpretation by this document alone.
The comparison with Colorado SB26-189 is limited to inspected clauses; it does not resolve all statutory applications or legal conflicts.
The docket comments and any final disposition were not accessible in this activation.
No provider behavior, model outputs, consumer effects, compliance cost or enforcement outcome was measured.

technical.claimed_result: The Commission proposes that undisclosed ideological output steering may violate Section 5 even when a provider says it is complying with state law, and that a conflicting state requirement may be impliedly preempted. This remains the agency’s proposed legal position.
technical.demonstrated_result: The FTC published the proposal and solicited public comment; the agency release records a 2-0 vote authorizing the Federal Register notice and a July 31, 2026 comment deadline. No final policy, adjudicated preemption or provider response is established.
technical.mechanism: The FTC proposal applies its stated Section 5 deception framework to AI companies’ representations about system objectives and accurate outputs. It argues that undisclosed steering toward objectives users did not request or expect may be deceptive, and that this federal interpretation can conflict with state requirements compelling output alterations.
technical.regime: U.S. federal consumer-protection policy proposal, File P264200 / Federal Register document 2026-13628, published July 1, 2026; comment deadline July 31, 2026. Comparison includes Colorado SB26-189 signed May 14, 2026. Legal status and effects remain unadjudicated/unmeasured.
technical.strongest_baseline: The proposal invokes established Section 5 deception principles; Colorado SB26-189 is a separate enacted state law concerning covered automated decision technology and consequential decisions. No court or Commission adjudication in the inspected sources resolves their interaction.

brief.title: FTC proposes a Section 5 theory for undisclosed AI output steering
brief.why_it_matters: If adopted or applied, the proposal could affect how AI providers describe model objectives and how federal consumer-protection authority interacts with state rules for consequential automated decisions. Its legal theory remains a proposed agency position; the precise interaction with state law and any effect on model behavior or compliance are not established.
